pedagogy.summary:
• Age / Topic — 12–14; Hazard Assessment & Evacuation (CONCEPTUAL, META/decision-under-uncertainty): probabilistic hazard assessment (eruption recurrence intervals, fault slip rates); how observatories monitor deformation/gas/seismicity to set alert levels; WHY communities stay near hazards (fertile volcanic soil, poverty, cultural/ancestral ties); and the ethics, politics and SOCIAL-JUSTICE dimensions of who bears risk and who decides to evacuate.
• Standards — UK (DfE): the science of hazards/monitoring links KS3 (Earth structure, waves); the risk/vulnerability/social-justice dimension is cross-curricular — KS3 Geography (natural hazards, why people live in risky places, responses) and Citizenship/PSHE. Not a KS3 science-only topic. State tier: DEFERRED.
• Standards — US (NGSS, ANCHOR): MS-ESS3-2 '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2]' — clarification (VERIFIED verbatim): some hazards (volcanic eruptions, severe weather) are preceded by phenomena allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes 'occur suddenly and with no notice, and thus are not yet predictable'; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies. DCI ESS3.B (mapping hazard history to forecast; mitigation) is knowledge-based here (verified:false). Builds on 4-ESS3-2 (VERIFIED earlier) generate-and-compare mitigation solutions.
• Operational details — TWO intertwined payloads. (1) QUANTITATIVE: probability is not prediction — recurrence intervals and slip rates give a likelihood/return period, not a date; a '1-in-100-year' event can happen next year; alert levels translate monitoring data into staged decisions. Be precise that volcanoes often give warning signs while earthquakes do NOT (per MS-ESS3-2). (2) HUMAN/ETHICAL: evacuation is a decision under uncertainty with real costs — a false alarm has economic and trust costs; a missed evacuation costs lives; people stay for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture), and disaster risk falls unequally (social justice). Prerequisite assumed: Earthquake-Resistant Design (mitigation framing). This topic feeds Supervolcanoes and Mass Extinctions (scaling the assessment up).
• Checkpoint — Tier C (formal/model-based + reasoned judgement): given monitoring data and a probabilistic assessment, the child WEIGHS an evacuation decision — distinguishing probability from certainty, articulating the cost asymmetry of false-alarm vs missed-warning, and accounting for WHY people stay and who bears the risk — reaching a justified position rather than a single 'correct' answer.
bestPractices: Separate probability from prediction explicitly: a recurrence interval / slip rate gives a likelihood or return period, NOT a date — practise reading '1-in-N-year' correctly (it does not mean 'safe for N years').
Use MS-ESS3-2's own distinction: volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (so alerts are possible), earthquakes strike without notice (so preparedness, not prediction, is the defence).
Teach the decision as a cost-asymmetry problem: false alarm (economic loss, eroded trust, 'cry wolf') vs missed warning (deaths) — there is no cost-free choice, only trade-offs.

Take the 'why do people stay?' question seriously and non-judgementally: fertile soil and livelihoods, poverty and lack of alternatives, deep cultural/ancestral ties — staying is often rational, not ignorant.

Foreground social justice: vulnerability is unequally distributed; the poorest and most marginalised typically bear the greatest disaster risk and have the fewest options — use real cases to make this concrete.

Ground it in authentic decisions and roles (observatory scientist, mayor, resident, aid agency) so students reason WITH the uncertainty and the human stakes rather than treating hazard as a purely technical problem.
keyRepresentations: Recurrence-interval / probability timeline: return periods and the (mis)reading of '1-in-100-year' — the core quantitative literacy rep.
Alert-level ladder (e.g. green→yellow→orange→red) mapping monitoring signals (deformation, gas, seismicity) to staged actions.
Decision matrix of the evacuation call: rows = evacuate / don't, columns = eruption happens / doesn't, cells = the four outcomes and their (asymmetric) costs.
Vulnerability map: overlay of hazard zone with population, poverty, and infrastructure — showing risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability, not hazard alone.
Stakeholder panel: scientist / official / resident / aid worker viewpoints on the same evacuation call, exposing the value conflicts.
commonMisconceptions: 'Scientists can predict exactly when a volcano/earthquake will strike.' — Assessment yields probabilities and (for volcanoes) precursor-based alerts; earthquakes are not yet predictable — probability is not a date.
'A 1-in-100-year event won't happen for 100 years / just happened so we're safe.' — Return periods are long-run averages; the event can occur in any year, including consecutive years.
'People who live in hazard zones are just ignorant or foolish.' — They usually stay for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture); dismissing this misreads the whole risk problem.
'The safe choice is always to evacuate.' — Evacuation has real costs (economic, health, trust); false alarms erode compliance with future warnings — the decision is a genuine trade-off.
'Natural disasters affect everyone equally.' — Risk is socially uneven; the poorest and most marginalised bear disproportionate exposure and have the fewest means to prepare or recover.
'Monitoring/technology removes the risk.' — It reduces and informs, but cannot eliminate uncertainty; decisions must still be made without knowing the outcome.

learn.summary: For ages 12–14, this topic teaches hazard assessment and evacuation as a judgement under uncertainty with competing human values. Two intertwined payloads: (1) a quantitative strand — probability is not prediction: recurrence intervals and fault slip rates give a likelihood or return period, not a date; observatories translate ground deformation, gas emissions and seismicity into staged alert levels; volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (so alerts are possible) while earthquakes strike without notice; and (2) a human/ethical strand — evacuation carries asymmetric costs (a false alarm brings economic loss and eroded trust; a missed warning costs lives), people stay near hazards for rational reasons (livelihood, poverty, culture), and disaster risk falls unequally. The core activity is an in-role deliberation reaching a defensible position rather than a single correct answer, supported by quantitative risk-literacy practice.

activities.title: The evacuation call: reasoning in role under uncertainty
feedback: If the learner treats the decision as having a single correct answer, probe: 'What would change if you had to answer to the 40,000 people either way?'

If the learner dismisses residents as ignorant or foolish, redirect: 'What rational reasons might someone have to stay — livelihood, poverty, ancestral ties? Does staying make the risk their own fault?'
If the learner says the safe choice is always to evacuate, ask them to name who bears the cost of a false alarm versus a missed warning, and whether those are the same people.
If the learner speaks as if the scientist can predict the eruption, prompt them to restate the data as a probability with warning signs, not a prediction of when.

If the learner judges a false-alarm outcome as proof the scientists failed, separate the quality of a decision from its luck: a sound call given the available information can still be followed by no eruption.
activities.rationale: The defining payload is weighing evidence and competing values with no single correct answer. An open, unscripted dialogue affords interactive probing and lets the learner articulate and defend a position in real time — an observable affordance a static artefact lacks — though this reflects catalog fit rather than demonstrated comparative efficacy, so other media are not claimed to be incapable of building the skill. The MS-ESS3-2 distinction (volcanoes forewarned, earthquakes sudden) and the socially uneven nature of disaster risk give the role-play its authentic content.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.

Disaster risk is socially uneven (risk = hazard × exposure × vulnerability); communities stay near hazards for fertile soil, livelihood, poverty, and cultural ties; evacuation decisions carry asymmetric false-alarm vs missed-warning costs.
learnerActions: Take the role of a volcano-observatory scientist briefing a mayor: the monitoring data is ambiguous — gas emissions and tremor are rising, but could fizzle out. State out loud whether to recommend evacuation and justify it.

Respond when the mayor presses back in role: 'If I evacuate 40,000 people and nothing happens, I've wrecked the harvest, cost millions, and no one will believe the next warning — are you sure?' Articulate that this is a probability, not a prophecy.
Face a lifelong resident who refuses to leave — this volcanic soil feeds their family and their grandparents are buried here. Engage their reasons seriously rather than dismissing them.
Hear an aid worker point out that it is usually the poorest, with nowhere to go, who die; factor equity into the position you defend.
Weigh the false-alarm cost (economic loss, eroded trust, 'cry wolf') against the missed-warning cost (lives) explicitly, naming that there is no cost-free choice.
Reach and defend a justified position, acknowledging you might be wrong either way.
activities.intendedInsight: Hazard assessment is not a calculation that outputs an answer; it is a judgement made under irreducible uncertainty, shaped by fairness and human stakes. One can make a good decision given the available information and still have an unlucky outcome.

activities.title: Risk dashboard: probability is not prediction
feedback: If the learner assumes a '1-in-100-year' event is 'safe for 100 years' or 'overdue' after 100 years, point to the repeated-trial tally: the event can appear in any run, including consecutive ones.
If the learner picks an alert level that ignores rising precursors, ask which monitoring signal they relied on and what it implies for staged action.
If the learner reads a false-alarm run as proof the scientists failed, revisit the tally: judge the policy over many runs, not one outcome.
activities.rationale: A simulation with repeated trials can model the numbers and the cost asymmetry so the probability-not-prediction lesson may land statistically; it is intended to pair with the dialogue rather than replace it, because reducing the ethical and social-justice deliberation to a payoff score would misrepresent the part that should not be a single number.
sourceClaims: Probabilistic hazard assessment uses recurrence intervals and fault slip rates to express likelihood/return period (not a date); observatories translate deformation, gas and seismicity into staged alert levels.

MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.
learnerActions: Read a recurrence-interval / probability readout and a set of monitoring signals (deformation, gas, seismicity) that climb over time.
Set an alert level (e.g. green → yellow → orange → red) by mapping the monitoring signals to staged actions.
Make an evacuation call, then see a simulated outcome reveal whether the event actually came that run.
Repeat the call across many runs and watch a running tally accumulate false alarms versus missed warnings, so the cost asymmetry is felt statistically rather than argued abstractly.
Toggle a vulnerability-map overlay (hazard zone with population, poverty and infrastructure) to see that exposure and vulnerability, not hazard alone, shape who is at risk.
activities.intendedInsight: A '1-in-100-year' figure is a long-run average and an annual likelihood, not a countdown; with imperfect prediction and the same monitoring information, lowering the alert threshold to cut missed warnings raises false alarms, and raising it does the reverse, so the best alert policy manages their asymmetric costs (better monitoring can reduce both, but not to zero).

activities.title: Reading the probability and the alert ladder (factual check)
feedback: For the gambler's-fallacy answer ('overdue, so much more likely now'), use a coin-flip analogy: within this lesson's constant-annual-chance model, a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'; a recurrence interval averages many unequal gaps, not a timer. (Some real fault models do let probability change with elapsed time, so this is a modelling simplification.)

For 'a 1-in-100 chance is so small it basically won't happen', separate probability from consequence: risk needs both, and compounding a small annual chance over a lifetime shows why preparing is rational.
For confusion between hazards, restate that eruptions and severe weather are often forewarned while earthquakes are not yet predictable, so earthquake defence is preparedness, not a date.
activities.rationale: A scored factual check suits misconception-critical knowledge (probability reading, signal-to-alert mapping, the volcano-vs-earthquake distinction), but it should stay on the factual layer; scoring the 'should you evacuate?' judgement would wrongly imply a single right answer, so that judgement belongs to the dialogue.
sourceClaims: MS-ESS3-2: '[curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2].' Clarification: [curriculum wording omitted; reference MS-ESS3-2] allowing reliable predictions, but earthquakes occur suddenly with no notice and are not yet predictable; data can include locations, magnitudes, and frequencies.

Probabilistic hazard assessment uses recurrence intervals and fault slip rates to express likelihood/return period (not a date); observatories translate deformation, gas and seismicity into staged alert levels.
learnerActions: Interpret statements like 'a 1-in-100 chance each year': decide whether elapsed time since the last event raises this year's chance. As a modelling assumption for this probability-literacy lesson, treat the annual chance as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time, so it does not rise simply because time has passed.
Match monitoring signals (ground deformation, gas, seismicity) to the appropriate alert level on the ladder.

Identify which hazards usually give precursors (volcanoes, severe weather) versus which strike without notice (earthquakes), and state the consequence for how each is managed (forecasting and alerts plus preparedness vs preparedness alone).
Use a tap-to-reveal vulnerability map or alert-level ladder as a reference for what each alert level means and what makes a community vulnerable.
activities.intendedInsight: Core probability literacy and monitoring facts underpin the judgement work: a return period is an average, not a schedule, and alert levels are a translation of data into staged action.

constraints: Separate probability from prediction explicitly: a recurrence interval or slip rate gives a likelihood or return period, not a date; '1-in-N-year' does not mean 'safe for N years'.

Treat each year's probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time as a modelling assumption for the probability-literacy lesson; the event is not 'saving up' and is not made more likely simply because time has passed. (Real geophysical hazards can show clustering and stress transfer, so independence is a simplification, not a physical law.)
Risk combines probability with consequence: a low annual probability is not negligible when the consequence is severe, so preparation can be rational even at low odds.

Use the MS-ESS3-2 distinction: volcanoes and severe weather usually give precursors (alerts possible), earthquakes strike without notice (preparedness, not prediction, is the defence). This verbatim clarification is a verified source; the broader mapping-to-forecast DCI detail was recorded as not re-verified.
Take 'why do people stay?' seriously and non-judgementally — fertile soil, livelihoods, poverty, cultural and ancestral ties — rather than framing residents as ignorant.
Foreground that disaster risk is socially uneven: the poorest and most marginalised typically bear the greatest exposure and have the fewest options; use real cases where possible.

The evacuation judgement should NOT be scored as if there is one correct answer; keep scoring to the factual probability-and-monitoring layer. The outcome of the dialogue is a defensible justified position.
A static vulnerability map or alert ladder is a useful reference for the components but does not by itself exercise the decision-making; use it to support, not replace, the deliberation.

The simulated repeated-trial tally and vulnerability overlay are illustrative mechanisms to make probability and exposure concrete; they are optional and should not flatten the ethical deliberation into a payoff score.
A good decision made under uncertainty can be followed by an unlucky outcome; judge warnings by the information available at the time, not solely by what happened afterwards.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Two of the four source claims (observatory/recurrence-interval mechanics; social-unevenness of risk and asymmetric evacuation costs) are marked verified:false in the row and attributed to material not fetched this session; treat the specific monitoring and disaster-risk details as unverified.
The MS-ESS3-2 clarification text is marked verified in the source; the DCI ESS3.B mapping-to-forecast detail was recorded as knowledge-based (verified:false).

The original diagnostic framing ('about a 1-in-100 chance each year, and on average erupts roughly every 100 years') is internally consistent, but learners may conflate the annual probability with the average interval; keep the two framings distinct when posing such prompts.

The source asserts individual years are 'roughly independent'; for real geophysical hazards this is a simplification (clustering and stress transfer can occur), so present independence as a modelling assumption for the probability-literacy lesson rather than a physical law. This qualification is also surfaced in the relevant activity and constraint, not only here.

Claims that an open dialogue is 'uniquely able' to teach the judgement and that a fixed artefact 'cannot' build the skill reflect catalog fit ranking, not established comparative efficacy; these have been reduced to affordance-based phrasing (interactive probing/real-time defence) without asserting other media are incapable.

Activity 1's intended insight was tightened: the trade-off (not the simultaneous occurrence of both error types) is what cannot be escaped under imperfect prediction, since an always-evacuate or never-evacuate policy eliminates one error type at the cost of inflating the other.

probeDeeper: Why might people keep living right beside an active volcano even after they understand the risk — and does that make the risk 'their own fault'?
An official orders an evacuation and the eruption never comes. Was that a bad decision? How would you judge it without knowing the future?
Earthquakes still can't be predicted to a day, but eruptions often give warning signs. What's the difference, and why does it change how each hazard is managed?
Who bears the cost of a false alarm, and who bears the cost of a missed warning — are they the same people?
assess.correctAnswer: The newspaper is wrong. A 1-in-100 annual chance is a probability, not a countdown — the volcano is not 'saving up' an eruption, and this year's risk is still about 1-in-100 no matter how long it has been. 'Every 100 years on average' is a long-run average across many unequal gaps, not a due date; each year is roughly independent.

errorPatterns.pattern: It's been 100 years, so the eruption is 'overdue' and much more likely now ('it's been building up / saving up').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Use a coin-flip analogy — a run of tails doesn't make heads 'due'; a recurrence interval is an average of many unequal gaps, not a timer.
errorPatterns.distractor: Yes — 100 years have passed, so a big eruption is overdue and very likely this year.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Says the risk rises simply because time has passed since the last eruption.

errorPatterns.pattern: A 1-in-100 chance is so small it basically won't happen, so there's no need to prepare ('the odds are tiny').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Separate probability from consequence (risk needs both); compound the annual chance over a lifetime and discuss why preparing is rational even at low annual odds.
errorPatterns.distractor: No — 1-in-100 is so small it basically won't happen, so nobody needs to prepare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Dismisses a low annual probability as negligible and ignores the huge consequence.

errorPatterns.pattern: If they evacuate and nothing erupts, the scientists were simply wrong and 'cried wolf' ('a false alarm proves they failed').
errorPatterns.nextMove: Weigh the missed-warning cost (lives) against the false-alarm cost (disruption); a good decision under uncertainty can still have an unlucky outcome.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Judges a warning purely by its outcome rather than by the decision given the information available.

responseLevels.gap: Treats the recurrence interval as a schedule ('overdue'), or dismisses the low probability as 'won't happen'; judges warnings only by their outcome.
responseLevels.full: Explains annual probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time, combines probability with consequence to justify preparation, weighs the asymmetric costs of acting under uncertainty, and applies it to a new case such as why an earthquake can't be dated while an eruption may be forewarned.
responseLevels.partial: Explains that 1-in-100 is a probability and 'every 100 years' an average, and lists monitoring signs and reasons people stay, but cannot combine probability with consequence to justify the evacuation decision or weigh false-alarm against missed-warning costs.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A volcano observatory says a volcano has 'about a 1-in-100 chance of a major eruption each year, and on average it erupts roughly every 100 years. The last big eruption was 100 years ago.' A newspaper prints: 'Scientists say the volcano is now overdue and will erupt this year.' Is the newspaper right, and how should we understand that '1-in-100 each year'?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child holding the 'overdue' / gambler's-fallacy model answers 'yes, it's due' — a different answer from one who treats the annual probability as roughly constant and independent of elapsed time. The reason tier separates '100 years passed so it must be now' from 'probability isn't a schedule'.
